caseNote: 가상 사례 (B2B 마케팅 에이전시, 사무용 의자 제조사의 영업팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 확인 가능한 실제 기업 사례 대신 계산을 따라가는 구성이 개념에 더 잘 맞아 company_story 대신 numbers_twist로 바꿨습니다.
insight: 매출은 사업의 '크기'를, 이익은 그 사업이 '할 가치가 있었는지'를 보여준다. 매출이 늘 때마다 뒤따라 늘어난 비용을 함께 봐야 한다.
misconception: 매출이 사상 최고면 사업도 가장 잘된 해다. 매출을 키우면 이익은 저절로 따라온다.

factChecks.note: softwareNote의 소프트웨어 사례는 일반적인 설명이며 특정 기업의 수치를 가리키지 않습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Record sales, no profit. How?
body: A 20-person marketing agency just had its best sales year ever: $3 million, up 50%.
The team celebrated. Then the owner saw what was left after paying everyone: $50,000. Last year, on far less work, it was $300,000.

image.label: Revenue is size. Profit is what stayed.
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실에서 직원들이 "Record year!" 배너 아래 축하 중이고, 구석에서 대표가 노트북 화면의 아주 작은 "$50,000" 숫자를 보며 당황한 표정. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Revenue rose from $2M to $3M. Did the agency do better?
body: You're the owner. Clients, projects and invoices all went up by half.
Before you decide on bonuses, what do you conclude?

options.text: Yes. 50% more sales is a great year
options.feedback: Sales show how much work came in, not what the work left behind. Bonuses paid on this number could wipe out what little was left.

options.text: Can't tell yet. First check what's left after all costs
options.feedback: Right. More sales only help if costs grew less than sales did. The next card shows they didn't.

options.text: Probably, as long as clients paid on time
options.feedback: Getting paid matters, but that's a question about cash. Even clients who pay on time can't fix work that costs more than it earns.

cards.title: Two years side by side.
body: Revenue rose $1 million. Costs rose $1.25 million. Most of the jump came from freelancers hired to cover a big new client. They cost more per hour than staff. A bigger office came next.

cards.title: Revenue vs profit
body: **Revenue** is all the money customers pay you for what you sell, before any costs. It's called the *top line* because it sits at the top of the income statement.
**Profit** is what's left after every cost is paid: staff, materials, rent, everything. It's the *bottom line*.
Revenue tells you how much business you did. Profit tells you whether that business was worth doing.

image.label: A tall top line shrinking down to a thin bottom line
image.brief: 깔때기 모양 인포그래픽. 맨 위 넓은 띠 "Revenue (top line)", 중간에 "Staff", "Freelancers", "Rent" 비용이 빠져나가는 화살표, 맨 아래 얇은 띠 "Profit (bottom line)". 맨 아래 띠를 강조색으로.

cards.title: Why the top line can rise while the bottom line falls.
body: Revenue and profit usually move together, until one of these happens:
list: **Price cuts to win volume:** more sales, less kept from each one
**Costs that grow faster than sales:** overtime, freelancers, rush shipping
**Step-ups in fixed costs:** a new office or manager arrives before the extra sales do
**Costly customers:** a big client that takes more time to serve than it pays for
cards.callout: Every extra dollar of revenue drags some cost behind it. The question is how much.
cards.softwareNote: A software company can post record subscription revenue while losing money, because sales staff, ads and servers grow along with it. Investors may accept that for a while, but they will ask when each new dollar starts leaving something behind.

cards.title: Many teams only see the top line.
body: A sales team is usually measured on revenue. A product team may be judged on units sold. Few teams see the costs their wins create in other departments.
So a team can have a record quarter that leaves the company poorer: a deal sold at a deep discount, a custom request that ties up the factory, free delivery the warehouse pays for.
Asking "what did this cost?" is part of the job, even when nobody measures it.

image.label: Sales can capture credit while the firm absorbs cost.
image.brief: 단면도처럼 나뉜 회사 건물. 위층 영업팀은 "Record quarter" 트로피를 들고 환호, 아래층 공장·창고·회계팀은 늘어난 박스와 청구서 더미를 나르는 모습. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Low profit isn't always a problem.
body: A business may choose thin profit on purpose, for example by hiring before demand arrives or opening a second site. That's an investment, not a mistake, if it's planned and has a limit.
Profit also isn't cash. A profitable year can still leave the bank account empty if customers pay late. That's a separate lesson.
And one year can mislead. Look at the trend over several years before you judge.

cards.title: Now you run a sales team.
body: You lead sales at a company that makes office chairs. Each chair sells for $100 and costs $70 to make and deliver. Your team's bonus is based on revenue.
Your biggest customer usually buys 1,000 chairs. They offer to buy 1,500 if you cut the price to $80.

options.text: Take it. Revenue rises from $100,000 to $120,000
options.feedback: Your bonus goes up, but profit falls from $30,000 to $15,000. The company makes 50% more chairs to earn half as much.

options.text: Show your boss both numbers, then offer a smaller discount
options.feedback: You keep the customer talking and protect the bottom line. At $90, the bigger order earns the same $30,000 profit on $135,000 of revenue.

options.text: Turn it down and keep the price at $100
options.feedback: This protects what each chair earns. But a flat no may lose a customer who would have accepted a middle price.

cards.title: Revenue is size. Profit is result.
body: Before you celebrate a record sales month, ask what it cost to get there.
**Try it today:** take your last two months or quarters. Write revenue and profit side by side. Did they move the same way? If not, find the cost that grew.
